https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.author: Andy Anderson
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.bottom_line: Expect a mix of crusts, wet snow, wind-textured snow, and a few pockets of soft snow in the backcountry. Pay attention to conditions as you travel, and change plans if you see signs of unstable snow or unexpected conditions. Even though avalanches may be unlikely, keep using best practices like traveling one at a time through avalanche terrain and regrouping in safe zones outside avalanche paths or runout zones.
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
Normal caution

In general, triggering an avalanche has become increasingly unlikely on a regional scale. The snowpack continues to gain strength during this period of warm, calm weather. Evaluate the snow and terrain as you travel and adjust your plans if you see any signs of instability. Signs of unstable snow might include cracking, collapsing, or maybe an unstable snowpit test result. These should be unlikely and isolated at best. Complex or extreme terrain may warrant wider safety margins and more thorough evaluation since an isolated tiny avalanche could have serious consequences, like pushing you into rocks, over a cliff, or into other consequential terrain. 

Recent weather has also created variable snow conditions across the region, including wet snow, wind-affected snow, some soft colder snow, and crusts. On the positive side, the previous winds and warm weather left very little soft snow on windward slopes. This lack of soft snow meant last night's winds had very little snow to transport, so problematic wind slabs of concerning size or distribution are not expected today.

Even though the likelihood of triggering an avalanche has decreased, it still makes sense to use best practices for traveling in avalanche terrain, like: 

  • Only put one person on a slope at a time while the others watch from a safe spot.
  • When you regroup, do so in safe spots outside avalanche terrain.
  • Plan an escape route before you commit to a slope.
  • Start with smaller, less consequential terrain before going into bigger terrain.   

For more best practices, check out this excerpt from Staying Alive in Avalanche Terrain.

forecast_avalanche_problems.discussion:
Sugary, weak snow near the base of the snowpack has slowly been gaining strength. Across the forecast area, the places where you can trigger a persistent slab avalanche have become increasingly isolated. There have been no avalanches reported since November 20th. That comes with a significant caveat—we have had limited observations from extreme terrain above 12k feet in elevation. While generally unlikely, steep, unsupported slopes and areas with shallow trigger points remain the places where you could cause a persistent slab avalanche. 

Although triggering an avalanche on this layer is becoming less likely, the consequences remain high. Any persistent slab avalanche triggered today would fail near the ground and involve the whole snowpack. Don't let the improving trend make you complacent, especially in complex terrain. If you venture into these areas, consider the consequences of triggering a large avalanche and give yourself a wide margin for error. When in doubt, use terrain choice to limit your exposure.
forecast_avalanche_problems.name: Persistent Slab
forecast_avalanche_problems.problem_description: Persistent Slab avalanches are the release of a cohesive layer of snow (a slab) in the middle to upper snowpack, when the bond to an underlying persistent weak layer breaks. Persistent layers include: surface hoar, depth hoar, near-surface facets, or faceted snow. Persistent weak layers can continue to produce avalanches for days, weeks or even months, making them especially dangerous and tricky. As additional snow and wind events build a thicker slab on top of the persistent weak layer, this avalanche problem may develop into a Deep Persistent Slab.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.bottom_line: A weak layer of snow at the base of the snowpack continues to linger and create concern that large avalanches could be human trriggered. Higher elevation North aspects harbor this weak layer. Avoidance is key, choose to travel through Southerly aspects or have thoughtful route selections to avoid areas where this weak layer persists.
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
• A strong inversion has been in effect this past week. Valley bottoms act as a cold sink  while warm air remains high in the mountains.( This is when we get those clouds over the  valley lakes ,Topaz, Bridgeport and Mono Lake).  Besides creating some pretty mornings on our drive in, this warm mountain air has been affecting our snowpack as well. It has not been below freezing at Leavitt Lake Snotel (9,600 ft) since the night of the 26th. Snow is settling and S faceing aspects with snow are becoming warm and sticky. Yesterday,I was able to view a S aspect in the Twin lakes area with  a small loose wet near a exposed rock band indicating the effects of the inversion and sun exposure.
  • We're also seeing in some zones, a layer of surface hoar that was buried during the low intensity wind event this past Sunday and Monday 11/22-23.  This particular layer is only buried an inch or two below the surface, but will likely pose a problem after our next snow cycle which may arrive this coming Sunday evening 11/29.
  • Just like shaking off the dust from skis and snowmobiles from a long summer, shake of the dust from your observation skills.  Send us a observation from your phone on the AVY app (Iphone & android). Snap a pick, send a few sentences and help us improve the forecast with your observations!
  • The BWRA may open December 5 to motorized use,  if the 108/Leavitt Lake Rd junction has the necessary 24" of snow.

forecast_avalanche_problems.discussion:
As the name suggests, weak snow "persists" at the base of the snowpack. The weak sugary snow is from the halloween storm that rotted out to become sugary facets. Now those facets are buried at the base of the snowpack. This weak snow with a slab on top is our concern. The Persistent slab problem is located on the Northerly aspects in upper elevations since the halloween snow was sheltered in those locations and never melted during the 2 week hiatus from snowfall. Instead it went through the faceting processes and remains as part of the snowpack structure.

BAC staff have been tracking this week layer with series of snowpit tests. We have continued to find unstable results with ECT and DTT tests with mixed results. Variables include  aspect, elevation and snow pack depth. ECTs have been shown propagation in shallower snowpacks where the "taps" have affected the weak layer. In areas with deeper and denser snow we have used DTT as we have been unable to trigger propagation with an ECT as it is unaffected due to the depth of the weak layer. Overall we have found signs that the weak layer is trending towards healing and bonding with the newer snow, but are still receiving unstable results. If you were to trigger an avalanche it would be very large.

Keep appropriate safety margins and avoid steep shaded terrain from mid elevation to the ridge tops. Treat this avalanche problem as guilty until proven innocent.

A section of the Tuckerman Ravine Trail through The Lip Area is CLOSED to all use until the route is snow-free. This section extends from Lunch Rocks to the top of the Headwall where it meets the Alpine Garden Trail. Only this section of the trail is closed. This annual closure is due to the magnitude of the crevasses and undermining, along with the severe consequences of a fall in this area. (36 CFR 261.55(a))

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
Expect warm conditions over the next several weeks to accelerate snowmelt. Read the Higher Summits Forecast and use your own observations to make informed terrain choices that minimize your exposure to springtime mountain hazards.

You can manage your risk and exposure to the following spring hazards by choosing when, where, and how you travel:

  • Snow holes & glide cracks: These openings in the snowpack can be very deep and large enough for a person to fall into. Look out for horizontal cracks in the snow and open holes around steep cliff bands. Give these areas a wide margin when traveling around them, and remember that these holes become bigger and more dangerous each day. In most cases, these openings have no reasonable exit until the snow completely finishes melting.
  • Icefall and rockfall: Over the years many people have been severely injured or killed by falling ice in Tuckerman Ravine. Periods of warm temperatures, intense sunshine, and rain can increase the risk of falling ice or rock. Look out for sections of ice that are looming above you and minimize your time underneath. Avoid spending time in high risk areas like Lunch Rocks or on the floor of Tuckerman Ravine in the fall line of ice above. 
  • Undermined snow: Meltwater flowing under the snowpack erodes away the snow above, creating thin bridges of snow that can collapse. These will emerge at the tops of gullies and in areas that have streams running, like the brook feeding the Little Headwall. The sound of running water can sometimes be heard under the snow and is a good indicator of this hazard.
  • Refrozen snow surfaces: Icy, hard snow creates a high-risk scenario for anyone traveling in steep terrain. A mountaineering mindset and tools, including crampons, ice axes, and helmet, are necessary to prevent a dangerous fall in steep terrain. Elevation-specific temperatures, cloud-cover, night/day temperature fluctuations, and wind could cause rapid refreezing of snow surfaces. These conditions can occur fast and could cause uncontrollable falls in steep terrain, which have the highest winter fatality rate within the forecast area. 
  • Other people: Sunny, warm spring days draw crowds of skiers to ravines. Remain mindful of where and how other people are traveling around you.

You can read more about springtime mountain hazards here.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.bottom_line: You could trigger avalanches in some areas, especially at upper elevations. Avalanches may be small, but they can still push you through rocks and other hazards. To avoid early-season accidents, assess conditions carefully before stepping onto steep slopes.
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
Challenging access and limited snow coverage may make it difficult to find areas where avalanches are possible, but don’t let that stop you from taking conditions seriously. If you reach terrain with enough continuous snow to produce avalanches, recognize that dangerous conditions may exist. Be confident in your ability to assess the snowpack conditions and when in doubt, default to more conservative decisions.

Uncertainty is an important factor as we’re heading into the weekend.  In many upper elevation areas, there is enough snow to produce avalanches. In more specific areas, like Washington Pass, the Baker area, and Crystal Mountain, there could be enough snow to produce small avalanches even at mid elevations. In recent days, observers have reported triggering avalanches and seen other telltale signs of instability, like long shooting cracks. We believe that there is more of a concern at upper elevations, where there is more snow and information is limited. 

Keep the following points in mind as you head into the weekend:

  • Small avalanches can have big consequences. Even a small avalanche can be treacherous, dragging you through rocks or other terrain traps. 
  • If you’re traveling over smooth or mostly smooth, steep, snow-covered surfaces, expect that this is where you could trigger an avalanche. It’s up to you to assess the stability of that slope. 
  • Watch for signs of unstable snow, such as recent avalanches, whumphing collapses, long shooting cracks, or rollerballs. 
  • Enjoy the sunshine that we expect on Saturday, but beware changing snow conditions. Wet avalanches could become a problem on steep slopes with enough snow cover. Snow conditions could change quickly. 

The forecast is for generally pleasant weather through the weekend, but precipitation and changing snow conditions are expected Monday, before the next General Avalanche Statement comes out. 

During the run up to winter, NWAC forecast staff will monitor snow, weather, and avalanche conditions and issue an updated Snow and Avalanche Discussion at 6 pm every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday until daily avalanche forecasts begin. 

What did you see? Share your observations with NWAC and the backcountry community.

Avalanches may be small, but they can still push you through rocks and other hazards. To avoid early-season accidents, assess conditions carefully before stepping onto steep slopes.
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
Challenging access and limited snow coverage may make it difficult to find areas where avalanches are possible, but don’t let that stop you from taking conditions seriously. If you reach terrain with enough continuous snow to produce avalanches, recognize that dangerous conditions may exist. Be confident in your ability to assess the snowpack conditions and when in doubt, default to more conservative decisions.

Uncertainty is an important factor as we’re heading into the weekend.  In many upper elevation areas, there is enough snow to produce avalanches. In more specific areas, like Washington Pass, the Baker area, and Crystal Mountain, there could be enough snow to produce small avalanches even at mid elevations. In recent days, observers have reported triggering avalanches and seen other telltale signs of instability, like long shooting cracks. We believe that there is more of a concern at upper elevations, where there is more snow and information is limited. 

Keep the following points in mind as you head into the weekend:

  • Small avalanches can have big consequences. Even a small avalanche can be treacherous, dragging you through rocks or other terrain traps. 
  • If you’re traveling over smooth or mostly smooth, steep, snow-covered surfaces, expect that this is where you could trigger an avalanche. It’s up to you to assess the stability of that slope. 
  • Watch for signs of unstable snow, such as recent avalanches, whumphing collapses, long shooting cracks, or rollerballs. 
  • Enjoy the sunshine that we expect on Saturday, but beware changing snow conditions. Wet avalanches could become a problem on steep slopes with enough snow cover. Snow conditions could change quickly. 

The forecast is for generally pleasant weather through the weekend, but precipitation and changing snow conditions are expected Monday, before the next General Avalanche Statement comes out. 

During the run up to winter, NWAC forecast staff will monitor snow, weather, and avalanche conditions and issue an updated Snow and Avalanche Discussion at 6 pm every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday until daily avalanche forecasts begin.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
Fast Off The Starting Gate

Today is the first 5-scale avalanche forecast of the season and we are right in the thick of it. Dangerous conditions matched with low snow coverage is a mean combination. Less than two weeks ago most terrain was completely bare of the snow. The exception was shaded, northerly aspects above 9,000’ where weak basal facets formed directly above a crust. Numerous avalanches were triggered during the first loading event a week ago. Expect more avalanche activity today as a heavier loading event stresses the poor snowpack structure. The dense snowfall has produced up to 1-2.2 inches of snow water equivalent (SWE) so far. An additional 2-6 inches of snow is possible today. 

The most dangerous conditions will be where you find the deepest snow coverage (wind-loaded, north facing). Be weary of the temptation to seek those steep, deeper slopes during this rapid loading event. Shooting cracks and collapses are an obvious sign of instability. Stick to lower angle, mellow terrain to manage the avalanche conditions and low snow coverage. This storm will cover copious amounts of buried obstacles and hazards. Stay safe and enjoy the fresh snow as we knock off the rust. A long winter awaits.

Wind typically transports snow from the upwind sides of terrain features and deposits snow on the downwind side. Wind slabs are often smooth and rounded and sometimes sound hollow, and can range from soft to hard. These avalanches will be more likely on wind-loaded slopes where the two avalanche problems overlap.

Clouds will begin to break by the afternoon.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.author: Eric Falconer

A relatively shallow and stable snowpack exists across the forecast zone, with the exception of high alpine terrain. Avalanche danger will likely rise over the coming days with the arrival of wind and snow. Watch for the five red flags of avalanche danger and remember when snow is the problem, terrain is the solution.

Daily avalanche forecasts will begin December 1. In the meantime, we will update this advisory and the observations page as conditions warrant.
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
Snow depths measure 29 inches at the Old Ski Bowl and 15 plus inches the Eddy Mountains. Exposed and shallowly buried obstables are abundant. Ski and ride with caution. 

When there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide. If venturing into the backcountry, approach avalanche terrain with caution. Be alert for signs of instability like recent avalanches, blowing snow, and shooting cracks and choose mellower terrain (>30 degrees) if you see them. Early-season avalanches in low-snow conditions can bring the increased hazard of collision with rocks and trees. As always, even small avalanches can have serious consequences in extreme terrain. 

Remember that when the snowpack is in question, terrain is the answer—opt for slopes that are low-angled (less than 30 degrees) and not connected to steeper terrain.

Climbers: Be prepared for challenging, winter-like conditions on the upper mountain, including heavy snow, extreme winds, and whiteouts. 

Early-Season Reminders and Resources: Traveling with a partner increases your margin of safety. Carry a beacon, shovel, and probe and know how to use them. Now is a great time to get your gear ready for the season, including the ten essentials, and hone your avalanche safety skills. Rescue practice is a productive early season activity. There are many excellent online avalanche education resources available to refresh your avalanche knowledge, such as this tutorial from the National Avalanche Center.

New snow last night increased the avalanche danger. Skiers, snowmobilers, ice climbers, hunters, and hikers should be cautious of steep, snow-covered slopes today and this weekend. 

Today’s new snow will add more weight to any buried weak layers, and create potentially unstable wind slabs where it is drifted into thicker, stiffer slabs. To start the season, our data is limited on specific locations of where persistent weak layers exist. This higher uncertainty requires more conservative decision making.

A layered snowpack exists at middle and upper elevations throughout the forecast area, with 1-3 feet of snow already on the ground prior to last night’s storm. On some slopes there are buried persistent weak layers which contributed to a skier-triggered avalanche last week in the Gallatin Range (observation). Additionally, Big Sky Ski Patrol triggered many persistent slab avalanches over the last week during mitigation work, including several yesterday after strong winds formed hard slabs over weak, faceted snow. There have been a number of other avalanches triggered in the last 10 days (The Sphinx, Sacajawea Bowl approach, Frazier Basin) and more earlier this fall (avalanche activity list). 

In the Madison and Gallatin Ranges, where 6-8” of new snow fell, avalanches are likely and conservative route selection is advised. Choose terrain less than 30 degrees steep and avoid wind-loaded slopes. Avalanche danger is CONSIDERABLE in the Madison Range and Gallatin Range.

Where slightly less snow fell (3-5”), in the Bridger Range and near Cooke City, West Yellowstone, and Island Park, the likelihood and potential size of avalanches is lower, but you should remain cautious. If you choose to ride or cross steep slopes, select slopes without fresh drifts, and without terrain traps that increase the consequences of a slide, such as cliffs, rocks, or confined gullies. This time of year the shallow snowpack means terrain traps are more widespread due to more exposed rocks and logs. The Avalanche danger is MODERATE in the Bridger Range, and near Cooke City, West Yellowstone, and Island Park.

New snow and strong winds are building slabs and drifts that may be sensitive to your weight. Avalanches failing under the newest snowfall, as well as those breaking on weak snow buried deeper in the snowpack, are possible, especially in areas with favored snowfall amounts. Sensitive wind drifts are most likely above 8,000' on slopes that held snow prior to these storms. You can lower your risk of encountering an avalanche by avoiding steep slopes where wind has stiffened the snowpack. Cracking and collapsing are clear indicators that conditions are unstable. 

We will update this General Avalanche Information on or before Tuesday, December 1st.
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
The tide is slowly coming in, and access to our snowy peaks is increasing with each passing storm. After last season, we're all hungry for snow. It's easy to lose sight of the fact that the season is long and as per usual, our early-season snowpack hosts a number of problematic weak snow layers. Turn your avalanche brain on, keep it tight, and  pay close attention to the snow you are traveling through. Read on for more information:

NEW SNOW: Fresh snow and strong winds will quickly combine to build slabs today and overnight tonight. These winds will shift direction throughout the next three days, depositing slabs in unusual locations in addition to the places you normally find them. The new slabs will be deposited on a variety of weak snow surfaces that developed throughout several days of dry weather and clear skies. On colder, shaded slopes prior to this storm, you'd find piles of surface hoar and weak facets at the surface. As you wrap around to warmer, sunnier slopes, you'd find a mix of crusts and facets, with sun crusts on the warmest slopes. Any of these surfaces can make for a reactive weak layer. These layers can break wider than you might expect and may be triggered remotely. 

OLD SNOW: In addition to the new batch of slabs that are forming at the surface, we have a layer of weak snow buried near the base of the snowpack. This snow produced several natural and human-triggered avalanches earlier this month during periods of active loading, and despite the snowpack remaining relatively shallow below 9,000'. This weak snow may reawaken due to loading from the current storm system. Smaller slides involving just the new snow may step down and trigger much larger slides as they travel downslope. 

OBSERVATIONS: Read ours and share yours here! We've been receiving some great observations from folks, so keep it up. Submitting an observation helps you process what you saw on your day out, informs other users, and improves our forecasts.

EDUCATION: Now is a great time to learn about snow and avalanches or refresh your knowledge. Watch a recorded class, seminar, or tutorial on our YouTube channel, or check out the great educational resources at avalanche.org.

RESCUE GEAR:  Test, inspect, and practice with your rescue equipment. This includes checking your probe for wear and tear, refreshing your beacon batteries, making sure your shovel is functional, deploying your airbag, and generally making sure everything is in working order. Did you already do that? Nice job! Now grab a friend and practice beacon rescue!

Mountain Weather – Friday, November 27 through Monday, November 30

A second large storm in less than two weeks is underway. Snow began early today under westerly flow, with a stronger push of moisture arriving tonight along a cold front. As of noon on 11/27, the mountains have received 3-6 inches of snow above 7,000 feet. Moderate to strong winds over 40 mph are likely tonight. By Saturday morning, the flow shifts to the northeast, and snowfall eases into a brief lull Saturday afternoon. The flow swings back to the west and southwest Sunday, bringing another round of snow into Monday before clearing out Monday night. Snow falls mainly above about 7,000 feet, with a couple of inches possible down to 6,000 feet and little accumulation in the valleys. Expect 9–14 inches in the mountains by Monday. 

Sawtooth & Western Smoky Mountains
The Stanley area could be the wettest spot in the forecast area tonight, possibly topping an inch of water. Highs reach the mid-30s °F today and the low 30s °F Saturday, with Saturday night lows in the low-to-mid teens °F. Snow returns Sunday and continues into Monday, with highs in the mid-30s °F.
Estimated snowfall: 9–14 inches by Monday above about 7,000 feet.

Galena Summit & Eastern Mountains
Near Galena Summit, highs are in the low 30s °F today and the upper 20s °F Saturday, with lows in the mid-teens °F. Up to 6 inches could fall at the pass tonight into Saturday morning, with more Sunday into Monday.
Estimated snowfall: 9–14 inches by Monday above about 7,000 feet.

Soldier & Wood River Valley Mountains
Valley highs reach the low 40s °F today, so expect rain or drizzle in the valleys and snow up high. Saturday clears and cools, with valley highs in the upper 30s °F and lows in the mid-20s °F. Precipitation returns Sunday into Monday, with valley highs in the upper 30s °F.
Estimated snowfall: 8-12 inches by Monday above about 7,000 feet; little accumulation on valley floors.

Banner Summit
Highs are in the low 30s °F today and near 30°F Saturday, with lows in the upper teens °F. Snow returns Sunday and continues into Monday, with highs in the low 30s °F.
Estimated snowfall: 8-12 inches by Monday.

Outlook: Mostly dry weather and seasonable temperatures return Tuesday through midweek.

I often make the joke that Bend is never as excited about backcountry riding as when there is 6 inches of snow on the cinder cone!  Sure enough there is snow in the high country and folks have been getting out sliding around.  The Central Oregon Avalanche Center is scheduled to begin daily avalanche forecasting on December 1.  By no means does this mean that avalanches aren't possible before then.  If you are headed out to make turns or ride in avalanche terrain, you should consider the possibility of avalanches.  This means doing all the same things you should be doing later in the winter:  carrying avalanche rescue gear, using thoughtful travel techniques, and assessing the snowpack.  When the snow is shallow, folks might be looking for where it's blown in a bit to hit the least rocks.  These wind blown deposits can also be the most likely places to find significant avalanches during the early season.  If you are thinking about heading out, check out both our observations page as well as our weather station map for conditions.  

Hopefully the snow will continue to pile up, and we'll have great riding by the time we begin operating.  In the meantime, be careful out there; of avalanches, but maybe more so of rocks, logs and other snow snakes.  Be patient.  Snow is exciting, but even our worst winters are long.  The avalanche center has lots of pre-season events scheduled to help you build enthusiasm for the season!  Here is a link to our events page:  https://coavalanche.org/pages/events.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
We will update the General Avalanche Information Product through the fall. We will begin regular forecasting when there is enough to travel, ski, and ride. 

A stretch of dry but windy weather is forecast through the beginning of next week.  An active period of weather during the middle of the month brought several storms (November totals: 26 inches of snow and 2.2" snow water equivalent SWE) to our mountains. This snow, along with periods of wind, has built stiff cohesive slabs on top of old weak snow from October storms at upper elevations near and above treeline. At these upper elevations is where you'll find the deepest snowpack (2 to 3 feet) as well as the persistent slab avalanche problem. Below treeline at lower elevations, coverage is still thin, and ground hazards like rocks and downed trees remain the biggest problem.

As we push further away from the last loading event, triggering a persistent slab avalanche will become more stubborn, but the overall poor snowpack where stiff cohesive slabs rest on top of fragile weak facets still exists, especially at upper elevations that are impacted by wind. Another round of strong winds is forecasted Saturday and Monday, which will strip and scour some slopes as well as load and press others into harder, supportable slabs. Harder slabs feel good underfoot, but the concern is collapsing weak faceted snow beneath these slabs to trigger an avalanche.  Identifying slopes where this snowpack structure potentially exists is not that difficult right now, as these slopes will be most enticing to want to ski and ride and are found at upper elevations on northerly, east, and some cross-loaded west gullies. Shooting cracks, or loud audible collapses, may or may not be present; take the time to dig a quick pit to identify if this strong-over-weak snowpack structure exists. It's possible to remotely trigger an avalanche from the flats below, or a distance away, with any avalanche potentially being large enough to injure or bury you. 

Looking ahead, this extended dry period to end the month will continue to promote faceting in the overall shallow snowpack. Near-surface faceting will be the most obvious in travels, but we're seeing advanced faceting and depth hoar develop closer to the ground. This will provide great weak layers for what looks to be a pretty active weather period for the first couple of weeks of December. Thicker hard slabs on the surface will have the ability to hold more of a load when we do get snow. There's still lots of details to be sorted out with these systems, but the persistent slab problem won't be going away anytime soon. 

Below treeline, the coverage is still very thin (1- 2 feet) as early-season conditions exist. Downed trees, rocks, and stumps sit just below the snow surface and are hazardous on their own. If you're heading out to the high peaks, go in with an early-season mindset and expectations, as the season is just getting started. 

TAC has begun reopening for the 2026-2027 season and is optimistic about a better snow year than we've seen over the last two. We will continue the General Avalanche Information Product as the early season snowpack evolves and will begin regular forecasting when conditions warrant. In the meantime, here are some resources as we wait for more snow.

  • The Avalanche Hour Podcast

A quick and intense storm impacted all zones last night bringing 6" of new snow to Anchorage, accompanied by strong easterly ridgetop wind. Although natural avalanches are unlikely today, there are good chances a person could trigger an avalanche up to 1.5' deep in new and windblown snow. This problem is typically found in high alpine bowls and below ridgelines, but windspeeds were strong enough to build wind slabs lower on slopes than normal. The safest thing is to give the snow some time to stabilize before getting out onto steep slopes.

Unless ridgetop winds pick up again, it should be more difficult, on Sunday, for a person to trigger an avalanche up to 1.5' deep in windblown snow. Once wind slabs become stubborn, they may let you get way out onto a slope before releasing. Choosing slopes with clear runouts will reduce the chances of a poor outcome if you get surprised.

Recent Avalanches: We are unaware of any recent avalanches in the front range, although we expect there were some natural wind slabs last night during the storm. 

Ridgetop winds are just calming down as of 5am this morning and It's hard to say how touchy conditions will be today. It doesn't take much snow and wind though to make an avalanche big enough to get us into trouble. Luckily, wind slabs are relatively easy to sus out and avoid because they look like "pillows" of snow and feel like firm snow over soft snow. They sometimes sound hollow if you tap your pole, skis or board onto them. If you see a shooting crack it means the snow needs more time to stabilize. Look for soft snow in wind protected areas to enjoy the new snow today.
forecast_avalanche_problems.name: Wind Slab
forecast_avalanche_problems.problem_description: Wind Slab avalanches are the release of a cohesive layer of snow (a slab) formed by the wind. Wind typically transports snow from the upwind sides of terrain features and deposits snow on the downwind side. Wind slabs are often smooth and rounded and sometimes sound hollow, and can range from soft to hard. Wind slabs that form over a persistent weak layer (surface hoar, depth hoar, or near-surface facets) may be termed Persistent Slabs or may develop into Persistent Slabs.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
As winter gets underway, our snowpack is starting to age and metamorphose. Previously wet, warm snow that fell in October has frozen, faceted, and crusted into its current shape. A few rounds of wind have formed breakable crusts and small but dense slabs at upper elevations. On other slopes, snow has become soft and sugary as it's slowly faceted. As we navigate this cold, dark part of the season, so does the snowpack, slowly faceting and weakening as it dries out and becomes rotten and sugary. While this process can improve riding conditions in the near term, in the long term it can lead to persistent avalanche problems. We're not tracking specific layers in the snowpack yet, as we haven't had enough new snow weight to cause trouble, but use caution when approaching steep slopes after rounds of new snow and wind, as these faceted layers can be protected and lead to surprising instabilities. As the snowpack ages and the weight of new snow accumulates on top, old crusts and wind slabs can re-awaken as new, less manageable avalanche problems. 

Dry Loose - There is a variety of snow surfaces across the forecast area, and new snow is likely bonding poorly to the surfaces below. If you are getting into extreme terrain, manage your sluff, and be aware of who is below you. These avalanches will be small in size, but could knock you down or cause injury. 

Glide Avalanches - A significant late-October snow fell on warm ground, leading to a widespread glide avalanche cycle. It has been two weeks since the last report of a glide avalanche, and we are likely out of the woods with this problem. However, if you see an open glide crack, consider choosing a route that avoids crossing under it, and avoid lingering below it. 

Early Season Conditions - While we're in significantly better shape than this time last year, the snowpack is still relatively thin and early-season conditions exist, especially in mid and low elevation terrain. Rocks, alders, and open water remain obstacles throughout the forecast area. Paired with the low light of late November, these could prove to be hazards to travel.

This year, we're launching our "Observer of the Month" award and will feature our most helpful observations with prizes and swag at every month's State of the Snowpack. Anyone can enter by submitting an observation and sharing what you're seeing at the pass.

forecast_avalanche_problems.discussion:
In the last 24 hours, Hater Pass has received about 8 inches of new snow accompanied by strong southeast winds (28 gusting 53 overnight on Hatch). Winds have transported snow, loaded slopes, and created fresh slabs in mid- and upper-elevation terrain. In many areas, new snow and wind slabs were deposited on weak, small-grained facets formed over the last couple of weeks. Slabs could be up to 1-2 ft deep, stiff enough to take you off your feet, and big enough to bury you.

As you climb in elevation, be on the lookout for:

  • Recent avalanches triggered by cornice fall or natural wind loading.
  • Dense or stiff drifts. 
  • Cracking, collapsing, or hollow-sounding snow.

These are signs that a slope has been loaded by the wind and clues that you have found an unstable slope, and you should seek lower-angle or non-windloaded terrain. Lower-angled, mid-elevation slopes will be the best bet for some safe, soft turns today. 

With 8 inches of new snow and tapering winds throughout the storm, it will be possible to find Loose Dry and softer Storm Slab instabilities in mid- and upper-elevation terrain. While these problems are likely to be much more manageable than the stiffer Wind Slabs at higher elevation terrain, continue to follow safe travel protocols, travel one at a time across suspect slopes, and choose slopes with open runouts. 

On many slopes, you will likely find a nice blanket of new snow, but it's those specific areas near ridgelines, along the edges of gullies, or alpine bowls that should give you pause before committing to slopes steeper than about 30 degrees. Wind drifts could be thin to thick, depending on the extent of the wind loading. With a weak surface below, avalanches may break wider than you expect and could be large enough to knock you off your feet or machine. Terrain traps, such as depressions, cliffs, or exposed rocks, could increase the consequences of even a small slide.

Early Season Update

Overall
Although winter has started on the San Francisco Peaks, KPAC is not issuing regular avalanche forecasts yet. We will issue snowpack summaries as conditions develop. Snow is currently shallow and spotty. In many places, falling on hidden rocks, stumps and deadfall is a bigger danger right now than an avalanche. That does not mean the snow is stable. Steep, wind-loaded and shaded slopes above treeline can produce small avalanches now, and even a small slide can carry you into rocks and trees or over cliffs.

Season so far
The Peaks have had several early storms. The first snow came at the end of September and melted within days. A light dusting followed in mid-October. On the night of October 24–25, about 6 inches fell at Snowbowl, and the resort reported about 17 inches of snow before the season started. Another 5 inches fell in mid-November, and Arizona Snowbowl opened a day early, on November 19. After two lean winters, a very strong El Niño is expected to favor the Southwest this season. We hope that’s right, but a promising outlook doesn’t make a good season.

What we’re watching
Early-season snow that remains on cool, shady high-elevation slopes are prone to faceting (becoming sugar-like) and potentially forming a poorly bonded weak layer. If that happens and new snow buries it, it can become a persistent weak layer that lasts long into the season. We’re watching north- and east-facing terrain near and above treeline closely. 

Before you go

  • Carry a beacon, shovel and probe and know how to use them. 
  • Now is a good time to evaluate your gear with a pre-season checklist. 
  • Come to our first Avalanche Awareness this season. Happening next Thursday, Dec 3rd, 6 PM at the Law Enforcement Administrative Facility (LEAF) Auditorium 

 

Share what you are seeing even a quick note helps us track conditions. Tag us @kachinapeaksavy, use the AvyApp, or visit our observations page.

This is our last forecast of the 2025/2026 season!

The spring thaw continues to dominate Douglas Island. The Powder Patch station at Eaglecrest has recorded above-freezing temperatures since April 26. According to snow pits dug this week in two different locations, the snowpack appears to be fully saturated and in isothermal conditions. Our primary concern remains wet loose avalanches, along with the potential for a cornice fall to trigger a deeper, larger avalanche. In pits on both Northerly and Southerly aspects, we observed old melt-freeze crusts with density and grain-size changes around 100 cm below the surface. This is potentially the bed surface where we have seen larger avalanches release this month.

Cornice failures have continued to be observed around Douglas Island. Even when they are not stepping down into larger avalanches, they can still produce significant amounts of wet debris. Give cornices a wide berth and stay aware of overhead hazards. As we continue to see rain on snow combined with warming temperatures, the potential for large wet slab avalanches still exists.

Please continue posting your observations to Coastal Alaska Avalanche Center, even if it is simply reporting good conditions. All information is helpful, especially as we transition out of regular forecasts.

forecast_avalanche_problems.discussion: Wet loose avalanches often start small but can grow large as they entrain snow. Wet loose avalanches are especially hazardous in steep exposed terrain and above terrain traps such as cliffs and gulleys. Signs of wet loose activity include wet saturated surface snow that feels unconsolidated, pinwheels and rollerballs on slopes, and snow shedding off rocks and trees due to warming.
forecast_avalanche_problems.name: Wet Loose
forecast_avalanche_problems.problem_description: Wet Loose avalanches are the release of wet unconsolidated snow or slush. These avalanches typically occur within layers of wet snow near the surface of the snowpack, but they may quickly gouge into lower snowpack layers. Like Loose Dry Avalanches, they start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. Other names for loose-wet avalanches include point-release avalanches or sluffs. Loose Wet avalanches can trigger slab avalanches that break into deeper snow layers.

forecast_avalanche_problems.discussion: Cornices are unpredictable and can fail without warning. Cornice failures can put a significant load on the slopes below them which can often trigger large avalanches.  When traveling on ridgelines, cornices often fail much further back from their edges than expected. Cornices should be given a wide berth when traveling on corniced ridges and time spent under cornices should be minimized. This month there have been many observed cornice failiures triggering  larger avlanches.
forecast_avalanche_problems.name: Cornice Fall
forecast_avalanche_problems.problem_description: Cornice Fall is the release of an overhanging mass of snow that forms as the wind moves snow over a sharp terrain feature, such as a ridge, and deposits snow on the downwind (leeward) side. Cornices range in size from small wind drifts of soft snow to large overhangs of hard snow that are 30 feet (10 meters) or taller. They can break off the terrain suddenly and pull back onto the ridge top and catch people by surprise even on the flat ground above the slope. Even small cornices can have enough mass to be destructive and deadly. Cornice Fall can entrain loose surface snow or trigger slab avalanches.

forecast_avalanche_problems.discussion: Wet slab avalanches occur when water penetrates the snowpack and causes a failure at a buried weak layer or interface. Solar radiation, which produces meltwater that percolates through the snowpack, can trigger wet slab avalanches, along with rain on snow events. Wet slabs are generally more destructive and more difficult to manage than wet loose avalanches; they can break widely and without clear warning signs.
forecast_avalanche_problems.name: Wet Slab
forecast_avalanche_problems.problem_description: Wet Slab avalanches are the release of a cohesive layer of snow (a slab) that is generally moist or wet when the flow of liquid water weakens the bond between the slab and the surface below (snow or ground). They often occur during prolonged warming events and/or rain-on-snow events. Wet Slabs can be very unpredictable and destructive.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.bottom_line:
Incremental loading over the past week has continued to increase snowpack depths at elevations above 5,000 feet.  As storms continue to move through the Idaho Panhandle and snowfall accumulates, areas of avalanche concerns will increase.  As you travel, pay attention to snowpack depth, slope angle, and the potential consequences of an avalanche.

The next planned fall update will be on December 4, 2026.
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
We will continue issuing general snowpack and avalanche information on Friday’s until the mountains get significantly more snow and access improves. We plan to transition to regular forecast operations sometime in December.

A mostly dry November has given way to a more favorable weather pattern over the past week, bringing much-needed snowfall to the mountains. The most recent storm, which arrived on Thanksgiving, came in on the warmer side, pushing the rain/snow line up to approximately 5,500 to 5,800 feet. Rain melted much of the existing snow below 4,000 feet, while areas above 5,500 feet received an additional 6 to 12 inches, depending on elevation and location. Earlier today, an IPAC field team found approximately one foot of new snow at 6,500 feet on Blue Mtn, in the southern Selkirks. Although coverage remains limited, the recent storms have started to build a more substantial early-season snowpack at upper elevations.

At upper elevations, where the snowpack is a little deeper, weaknesses within the snowpack are becoming easier to identify. For the most part, the snowpack consists of two distinct layers. The bottom portion is made up of older, mostly faceted snow that formed during the dry conditions earlier in November. The upper portion, generally 12 to 18 inches deep, consists of newer snow that has accumulated since November 20. This newer snow slab varies in character from one location to another. In most areas, it currently lacks the cohesion needed to produce avalanche activity. However, additional snowfall and wind loading could change that quickly by adding weight and creating a more cohesive slab over the weaker snow below.

It's still early in the season, so we'll continue to remind you: if you're heading into the mountains, bring your avalanche rescue gear, turn on your avalanche thinking cap, and stay aware of your surroundings.  For now, the areas of greatest concern are small, isolated, leeward terrain features above 5,500 feet where wind-drifted snow may be accumulating. You can manage your exposure by paying attention to snowpack depth, the slope angle of the terrain you're traveling on, and the consequences of an avalanche should one occur. Remember that even a small avalanche can have serious consequences, particularly where shallow snowpack, rocks, trees, or other terrain features are present. Early-season conditions can be deceiving, and careful terrain choices are your best tool for staying safe.

OBSERVATIONS:

We continue to prepare for the upcoming season and will post observations whenever we get out in the mountains. We encourage you to do the same whether hunting, hiking, bagging one last peak, or in search of the season’s first turns. Please share with us what you’re seeing out there, especially if you see or trigger any avalanches. Posting a picture, giving a brief summary of coverage or conditions truly helps make our products better.

Click HERE to submit an observation and share information with your local avalanche community. We appreciate the observations we have received so far!

In the meantime, take a moment to inspect your avalanche rescue gear – beacon, shovel, and probe. It's also a good time to refresh on your snow and avalanche training and consider signing up for an AVALANCHE CLASS.

---

Saturday offers a break in the active weather pattern before another low pressure system impacts the region Sunday evening into Monday.

Precipitation chances increase as the surface low approaches the Washington-Oregon coast and southwesterly flow engulfs the region. Snow levels Sunday night into Monday may vary widely across our forecast zones as a warm tounge of air accompanies the heaviset precipitation. Once again, snow levels are expected to climb to between 4,500 and 5,000 feet across our northern forecast areas and closer to 6,000 feet around the Silver Valley. All said and done, snow totals could range 4 to 10 inches and likely hinge on where the cold air wins the battle against the warmer air mass.

The  remainder of next week (Tuesday through Friday) looks to feature seasonal temperatures and ongoing opportunities of light, orographic snowfall.

Past Weather: The Thanksgiving Day storm brought much-needed snow to mid- and upper elevations throughout the advisory area. Unfortunately, the storm arrived warm and brought rain to locations below roughly 5500 feet (image 1, image 2). Favored weather stations in the Flathead Range and southern Glacier Park recorded 1+ inches of precipitation and 8 inches of settled snow at 6000 feet. Most other mid-elevation stations note 3-5 inches of settled snow and 0.5-0.8 inches of water. New snow totals at upper elevations are likely higher, but we don't have stations there that record snow data. After a lengthy absence, winds returned to the area, with the Aeneas Ridge station clocking 30+ mph for about 30 hours (image). 

Current/Forecasted Weather: A potent system moves into the Northern Rockies today and overnight, favoring areas south of Missoula (image) and southwest Montana. This should bring only light, scattered showers to our region. High pressure will build Saturday into Sunday, with mostly dry conditions expected before the next wave of moisture impacts us Sunday afternoon into Monday. Next week looks to remain unsettled.

Snowpack: The recent snowfall arrived warm and dense and is resting on a foot or so of less dense, colder snow that fell during the week of November 15 - 21. This has most likely resulted in an upside-down near-surface snowpack. Moderate to strong southwest winds over the past 36 hours have transported snow onto leeward aspects. Before Thursday's storm, plenty of snow was available for transport because the previous 10 days of light winds resulted in minimal wind drifting.  

Avalanche concerns: Below the snow line, Thursday's rain-on-snow event likely produced rollerballs and small wet loose slides. Natural dry loose and slab avalanches may have occurred above the snow line, especially on steep, wind-drifted terrain. 

Many slopes lack enough snow for a slab avalanche. As you gain elevation, the snowpack deepens, becomes layered, and can avalanche. This is especially true on wind-loaded, upper-elevation slopes where coverage is best. If you travel in areas where the surface snow is denser than the underlying snow, you may hear a whumpf as the weak layer (softer snow) collapses. Shooting cracks often accompany this collapse. These are signs of instability and may result in an avalanche if you are on a slope steep enough to slide. 

Observations: FAC is currently operating with minimal snowpack observations. If you get out this weekend, please let us know what you saw by submitting an observation here.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.bottom_line: With snow on the ground and more piling up, it's time to start thinking about avalanches. If you’re out hunting or hiking, you are as susceptible to avalanches as a skier or snowmobiler. When in doubt, stick to low-angle slopes. We’ll start issuing avalanche forecasts in December, as dictated by conditions. In the meantime, we’ll continue issuing periodic conditions updates like this one.
https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
Our snowpack has continued to grow over the past week, with the following weekly snow totals at middle to upper elevations:

Seeley Lake: 6 to 9” snow / 1.6” snow water equivalent

Rattlesnake: 5 to 9” snow / 0.7” snow water equivalent

Bitterroot: 4 to 13” snow / 1.2” snow water equivalent

Much of this fell during a storm over November 19-21, or last night (November 26), depending on location. Our next active storm cycle has arrived, with the heaviest precipitation and strongest winds predicted tonight (Friday, November 27). A Winter Weather Advisory is in place over much of our forecast region. By tomorrow morning, 24-hour forecast snow totals for higher elevation areas are:

Seeley Lake: 4 to 8” snow

Rattlesnake:  4 to 8” snow

Bitterroot: 8 to 17” snow

Expect considerably less precipitation below about 4500 feet.

Cooling temperatures will accompany this pulse of precipitation. So, hopefully our lower elevations will see snow too, not just rain. After a brief break tomorrow night (Saturday into Sunday), precipitation will continue through early next week, with snow up high and rain down low.

Note the wide range of forecasted snowfall amounts, particularly in the Bitterroot Range. Uncertainty in a weather forecast translates to uncertainty in avalanche conditions. If you travel in the mountains this weekend, you’ll have to be your own forecaster. More snow and wind mean more avalanche hazard. Remember the common adage, "if there’s enough snow to ride, there’s enough snow to slide". On that note, you don’t have to be sliding on the snow to be exposed to avalanches. Hunters, hikers, and dog walkers can also find themselves in avalanche terrain. When in doubt, you can avoid avalanches by avoiding steep slopes.

Don’t let the recent snow totals give you a false sense of winter - it's still thin out there. Most of last week’s snow fell on bare ground. Hazards associated with thin snowpacks, like rocks, trees, and stumps, can increase the consequences of even a small ride in an avalanche.

As we wait for more winter to appear, use this time to check your rescue gear. Make sure your beacon has fresh batteries, your probe isn’t frayed or cracked, and your shovel still fits together as designed. Replace your kit as needed, and don’t forget to practice!

We will continue issuing conditions updates as the snow piles up, and plan to start forecasting in December, once we have enough snow. You'll find the latest information at MissoulaAvalanche.org and on the new-to-us Avy App. If you are out in the mountains, we'd love to hear from you. Please take a moment to share a few photos or a short note on what you're seeing through the form on our observations page or the Avy App. This Thanksgiving, we’re thankful for everyone who submits observations.

https://api.avalanche.org/v2/public/prod.hazard_discussion:
Our snowpack has continued to grow over the past week, with the following weekly snow totals at middle to upper elevations:

Seeley Lake: 6 to 9” snow / 1.6” snow water equivalent

Rattlesnake: 5 to 9” snow / 0.7” snow water equivalent

Bitterroot: 4 to 13” snow / 1.2” snow water equivalent

Much of this fell during a storm over November 19-21, or last night (November 26), depending on location. Our next active storm cycle has arrived, with the heaviest precipitation and strongest winds predicted tonight (Friday, November 27). A Winter Weather Advisory is in place over much of our forecast region. By tomorrow morning, 24-hour forecast snow totals for higher elevation areas are:

Seeley Lake: 4 to 8” snow

Rattlesnake:  4 to 8” snow

Bitterroot: 8 to 17” snow

Expect considerably less precipitation below about 4500 feet.

Cooling temperatures will accompany this pulse of precipitation. So, hopefully our lower elevations will see snow too, not just rain. After a brief break tomorrow night (Saturday into Sunday), precipitation will continue through early next week, with snow up high and rain down low.

Note the wide range of forecasted snowfall amounts, particularly in the Bitterroot Range. Uncertainty in a weather forecast translates to uncertainty in avalanche conditions. If you travel in the mountains this weekend, you’ll have to be your own forecaster. More snow and wind mean more avalanche hazard. Remember the common adage, "if there’s enough snow to ride, there’s enough snow to slide". On that note, you don’t have to be sliding on the snow to be exposed to avalanches. Hunters, hikers, and dog walkers can also find themselves in avalanche terrain. When in doubt, you can avoid avalanches by avoiding steep slopes.

Don’t let the recent snow totals give you a false sense of winter - it's still thin out there. Most of last week’s snow fell on bare ground. Hazards associated with thin snowpacks, like rocks, trees, and stumps, can increase the consequences of even a small ride in an avalanche.

As we wait for more winter to appear, use this time to check your rescue gear. Make sure your beacon has fresh batteries, your probe isn’t frayed or cracked, and your shovel still fits together as designed. Replace your kit as needed, and don’t forget to practice!

We will continue issuing conditions updates as the snow piles up, and plan to start forecasting in December, once we have enough snow.
